title: Signs, orientation and reverse scoring
summary: A construct has no natural sign, so negatively worded items must be reverse scored with the scale endpoints before estimation, or reliability and validity results become meaningless.

body.text: Multiplying all weights of a block by −1 gives an equally valid solution: [[sign-indeterminacy]]. Software therefore orients each block, typically so that most loadings are positive, and SEM Lab warns when a loading is negative.
A negatively worded item ("I regret choosing this provider") correlates negatively with the other items of its scale. [[reverse-scoring]] flips it with the scale endpoints:

body.explanation: min and max are the endpoints of the response scale, so on a 1–7 scale x′ = 8 − x: 1 becomes 7, 4 stays 4, 7 becomes 1. Use the scale endpoints, never the observed minimum and maximum.

body.text: Forgetting it is not always visible in the paths. In the item-screening data, with the negatively worded item left as answered, its loading is −.81 and Cronbach's α of the scale collapses to .06, yet the path to loyalty is unchanged (.465), because Mode A simply gives the item a negative weight. Reliability and validity checks expose the problem; the structural results hide it.
In SEM Lab, mark the indicator as reverse scored and enter its endpoints, or create a reversed column in Data Lab. Do one or the other, not both.

mistake.title: Deleting a negatively loading item
mistake.text: A negative loading usually means a coding issue, not a bad item. Check the wording first; reverse score it if it is negatively worded. Reverse scoring with the observed minimum and maximum instead of the endpoints silently shifts the values.

tryIt.task: In this starter, indicator x3 is bound to the column x3_rev, a reverse-worded copy of x3. Run PLS-SEM and look at the warning and the loading of x3. Then mark x3 as reverse scored (scale 1–7) and run again.

starter.title: Two constructs with a reverse-worded item

checks.question: On a 1–5 scale, what is the reverse-scored value of a response of 2?

options.feedback: That subtracts from 5 only. The formula uses min + max = 6.
Multiplying by −1 flips the sign but leaves values outside the response scale; standardised results would agree, but IPMA and descriptive statistics would not.
Only the midpoint (3) maps onto itself.

checks.question: Why can a forgotten reverse scoring leave the PLS path almost unchanged while α collapses?

options.text: Mode A gives the unreversed item a negative weight, so the composite is exactly the same, but α assumes all items point the same way.
options.feedback: Correct. The composite absorbs the sign; internal-consistency measures do not.

options.text: Because the path coefficient ignores all indicators.
options.feedback: Paths are computed from construct scores, which are built from all indicators.

options.text: Because PLS automatically reverse scores items.
options.feedback: PLS orients blocks, not individual items. Item coding is the analyst's responsibility.

checks.explanation: Check loadings and reliability, not only paths.
